utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Madam Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can follow in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. David Cunningham with Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good morning to you too. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know that and I have no doubt that the Dutch journalist will be delighted to hear we are in open session for this witness as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good. It's unfortunate that some journalists don't appreciate the importance of having closed sessions in order to protect certain sensitive witnesses, without whom this Tribunal would not function.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's unfortunate. I do not have, as you know, as a Trial Chamber we do not have a PRO, the Tribunal has but this is as far as I can go on my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree. I think it's better not to comments too much on this except to say this. I agree entirely with Your Honour's remarks. It may not be known to the press that - or the world at large - that this area has a great deal of difficulties in respect of the differing nationalities and that's one of the problems and were they to be privy to the information which Your Honours are privy to and Defence, it might be a different matter. Your Honour, that's all I want it to say about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just very briefly deal with the motion -- I need to go into closed session on this, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were inviting criticism.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was. Private session, it's a confidential motion I've just seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to say that in the rush to get this witness to make the further statement, to look at documents because we weren't expecting him to testify until tomorrow, the extra documents that were produced by the witness from Petrovac who came up with this mass of documents, some of them were omitted and they are not in Your Honour's list and they are not on the Defence list. I don't think we will get to them before the break. They are important documents but we are going to arrange for copies of the extra documents to be made and handed out as we get to them. I'm sorry about that. It was my fault. I didn't notice that I'd missed a whole batch of the documents produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should add that this witness like the other witnesses has not been proofed in the sense that Your Honours know. Finally, Your Honours, I've spoken to Mr. Cunningham. Mr. Cunningham thinks he needs about two hours to cross-examine. Your Honours, this witness has a lot to get through, as you'll see from the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have not even managed to read --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's another witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- what I would have liked to read because that's voluminous.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. Your Honour, he's one who has a diary as well, as Your Honours have seen. Your Honours, there are two methods of approaching this. One is we could say, or Your Honours could say, you must finish him by tomorrow. And we can move the next witness up but there will be a gap before the last witness. He cannot be here to testify before the Thursday of next week. And the next witness we anticipate will certainly take two days. I'm in the hands of Your Honour. If I can't finish I could apply to put in both the statement and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, let's go through it slowly because -- this witness was scheduled to start tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the idea or the plan was to have him finish on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The idea was to have him finish on Monday, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. Then there was a witness on Tuesday and Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then the final witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thursday, Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thursday, Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I had in mind but we discussed this and we are quite open to accommodate both of you, if you require the time, but my idea initially was since we were starting with this witness today, that we would try to finish him tomorrow, so that at least he won't have to stay here over the weekend. Now, if you can live with that, that obviously would be my preference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If, however, between the two of you, you require more time, we are prepared to accommodate you. Yesterday, I was told, but I think it was a mistake, that you needn't worry that much about not finishing with this witness by Friday because there will not be any witness available for Monday in any case. So -- and I found that strange because any witness who needs to start on Tuesday necessarily would be here at the end of this week. So you tell me what you would like and we will accommodate you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can. Certainly, we could try and move the witness up with the assistance of the VWS who would have to bring him in on the weekend and he could start on Monday if we finish this witness tomorrow. He won't take more - we estimate - than two days for the whole thing. Therefore there would then be a spare day on Wednesday although we do have some bits and pieces to clear up. Again, Your Honour, I don't know how long the last witness will take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I don't know. I don't want to interfere in that but the subpoena was to the effect that he would be available to start giving evidence on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Thursday and Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, 31st and 1st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought it started from the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No it's the 31st, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: See how --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we see how we go and then perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. No problem on our part. And if you need to keep this witness here until Monday over the weekend and finish him off on Monday, we have no -- we haven't got a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour, because I think as Your Honours will see he's clearly a witness of some importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is a witness of some importance for sure, yeah. Like many others. All right? Just to make sure, I inquired about this, but we are in open session and no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No protective measures, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Madam Usher, could you bring the witness in, please? Mr. Cunningham, if, as we go along, you feel that the time you require for your cross-examination should be longer, you just let me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right? Thank you. I apologise to you, Mr. Cunningham, I did not ask you for your remarks about what Madam Korner said, namely that some documents she hasn't been able to hand over to you in time and that she will be making them available before the break or by the next session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have a problem with that. They are doing their best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you do have a problem then we will reserve your position and you will have an opportunity to cross-examine with -- the witness can some delay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that you can understand what I am saying in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You are about to start giving evidence in this case, which has been instituted and ongoing against Radoslav Brdjanin. Our rules require that you make a solemn declaration before you start giving evidence, a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Madam usher is going to hand you the text of the solemn declaration, that is equivalent to an oath, and that you will be -- that will be your undertaking with us. Please go ahead and read that solemn declaration aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a chair.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are a few things that I need to tell you before you start giving evidence. Number one is that the procedure that is followed here is pretty much similar if not identical to the procedure followed in most other courts of criminal jurisdiction elsewhere. Namely that you will first be examined, questioned, by the Prosecution, and in this case, the officer questioning you will be -- is Ms. Joanna Korner, whom you've met already and then she will be followed by Mr. Cunningham, who is the gentleman in the front row to your left, and he is representing Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin. We will -- we call that cross-examination. Your duty, pursuant also to the oath that you've taken here, is to answer all questions that are put to you as fully and as truthfully as possible irrespective of who is putting the question. In other words, you have no right to make a distinction between Prosecution and Defence. Your duty or responsibility is to treat them equally and answer all questions that are put to you. Answer all questions with this reservation, there may be instances where I can intervene and say, "sir, don't answer that question." But unless and until I say that, your obligation is to answer the question. There is another matter which is very important and which I need to talk to you about. When you were interviewed by the Prosecution, you were informed that you may well be a suspect, in other words that the Prosecution here, at the time you were being interviewed, may well have had evidence which could actually make you end up being charged. However, I am told and I'm assured now by Madam Korner that that is certainly no longer the case. In other words, that you are not a suspect and that you should take this into consideration obviously while you give evidence. However, if in the course of your testimony, questions are put to you, whether by the Prosecution or by the Defence, which you think, you believe, that if you answer, you would be exposing yourself to some criminal action, to some criminal proceedings, in other words if you think that by answering those questions you would be incriminating yourself, then you have a right to ask me not to answer those questions. We will discuss it and then we will decide whether you should answer the questions or not. The matter is regulated by our rules and I want you to feel comfortable knowing that you are protected throughout the entire testimony that you will be giving. But what is perhaps more important than anything else is that I'm telling you publicly here, in open session, that you are no longer a suspect in terms of our statute and of our rules. Do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Start with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think if the microphones could be pulled a little closer. The interpreter did not hear him say he had no questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, could you give your name to the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: My name is Jovo Radojko.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you born on the 1st of October of 1956 in Klenovac in the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac, as it was then called?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are you a Serb by nationality?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you presently a practising judge in the basic court in Derventa?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as a judge presently serving, was your appointment approved by the office of the High Representative in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you, sir, a little bit about your background. Is this right, that you completed first of all the higher administrative school in Zagreb in about 1981?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then you went to the political science faculty in Zagreb intending to become a journalist, but didn't complete that but went instead to law school?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in 1987, did you receive your diploma from the Zagreb University law school?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, did you work in Zagreb until in 1990 you passed the bar exam?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you worked as a secretary to begin with in a school intending to continue your education but then at the end of 1990, was there some kind of ethnic problems with you as a Serb working in a Croatian school and were you then invited to go and work in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And did you arrive in Petrovac at the end of 1990? After the multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when had you joined the SDS?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: In the course of 1990, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you joined the Croatian SDS party at that stage?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Petrovac, at the end of 1990, were you appointed secretary to the executive committee of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that at the invitation of the President of the municipal assembly, Mr. Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just to complete -- jump forward a little bit, Mr. Novakovic, was he actually killed during the course of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had you known Mr. Novakovic before you took up your appointment?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you come to Petrovac as a result of the invitation to become the secretary?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you, please, a little bit about Petrovac because you'd been born there and I think your family came from there. Was Petrovac, Bosanski Petrovac, aligned economically, politically and judicially to the municipality or the region, really, of Bihac?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And for what reason was that? Was it a geographical region -- reason, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Well, by and large, yes. I'd say it was the geographic one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think if we can just for a moment put up the map, I've forgotten what the number is now. The bigger map of the Balkans like that so we can remind ourselves where Petrovac was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, maybe just sometimes -- it's because -- P1956.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we can just home in on the part towards the left of the plan, we can see or we should be able to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, it's actually very unclear on this. Any way of focusing a bit more? Obviously not. I tell you what. Can we move it up slightly? No, no, I'm sorry, the other way, usher, down, sorry, down, down, down, down, down. And down a bit more, please. Thank you. Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you see -- I think we can see Bihac on the lefthand corner of the map, if we go in virtually horizontal line we can see Banja Luka and then Petrovac, which is not terribly clearly marked, I have to say, on this, we can see coming down from Bihac, just there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hope Your Honours can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We know where it is any way. We have seen this map before and Petrovac was precisely indicated by a previous witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. I just want to show the relative positioning with Bihac and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can see it here any way, so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I think it's right, is it not, that Bihac as a municipality in itself, had a majority of the Muslim nationality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Bosanski Petrovac, and you needn't bother about the figures because we've had them, had a majority of Serbs by nationality?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you, please, a document which is P5, dated the 26th of April, 1991, which you've looked at before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That is on my list, Your Honour. Could we have that please put up on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've seen this document before, dated the 26th of April, 1991, which is a decision on the separation of the Petrovac municipality from the Bihac intermunicipal regional association. Do you know why -- first of all, could you look -- is that -- do you recognise the signature of Mr. Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know why this decision was taken?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: There were several reasons for it. One of them was economic. The municipality of Petrovac was very much lagging behind some other municipalities in the region, economically, and therefore there was a serious demographic decline because of it. It had 32.000 inhabitants in 1931 and the figure was the same in 1991, except that in 1991, its population was 15.500. Its infrastructure was backward and therefore there were economic reasons in the first place. Secondly, as far as I can remember, the atmosphere at the time, there were also some political reasons. That is, by seceding, by separating, as far as I know, they wanted to bring some pressure to bear both on the centre in Bihac and the republican administration in Sarajevo, in order to render more topical, to put on the agenda the problems which were becoming serious, and already at that time ethnic -- interethnic tensions had begun to emerge. I think it followed in the wake of the events in the municipality of Korenica in Croatia. After that, a certain degree of interethnic tension emerged between the Serbs and the Muslims in the area. Emotionally, and well, through their propaganda, the Muslims Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. endorsed the action of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior, of the Croatian police, in the municipality of Korenica, and the Serbs were against it so as far as I can recall now, these were the first reasons and they were just that one drop too many which then, coupled with, compounded with the economic reasons, made them decide to go alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The Muslim members of the municipal assembly, did they object to this decision?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I wasn't always party to -- I didn't always participate in the sessions of the assembly and possibly I was not present at that particular session, because some of the Serb councilmen did not like me being present there and so that I was present only when I had to, as a member of the executive board, say when I was needed there to explain the legal aspects of some decisions, but what I can say is that from my recollection of the general atmosphere and the general views, be it of the Serb parties or Muslim parties or those parties which were ethnically mixed, that the Muslim councilmen, at least the councilmen representing the SDA, were explicitly against it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That same day, if you look now, please, at P1813, was a decision made in the assembly to join the community of municipalities of the Bosanska Krajina? And again, was that decision signed by Mr. Novakovic, as president of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: In my opinion, since I know Mr. Novakovic's signature, I'd say that this document is an authentic copy but whether it was taken that same day, I'm not sure, as I think that the dates on the top are different, but it would be logical for this decision to follow the previous decision, that is, chronologically, they should follow after that initial decision, even though it is not sure whether this is the 20th or the 10th of April, because there is a misprint here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, but I think if we look back at the first decision, we will see that has the number 162/91, at the end, and this one is 163/91 so it looks as though it follows on. All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Just as I have just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, sir. You can put that document away. Do you know whether or not anyone from Bosanski Petrovac attended the founding meeting of the -- this particular association of municipalities in Banja Luka a few days before this decision?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. As a matter of fact, I do not know whether somebody was present. Possibly, yes. If somebody was present, then it should have been Mr. Novakovic -- then it would have been Mr. Novakovic, and a councilman representing Serbs from Petrovac but I'd say that Mr. Novakovic in more -- in every likelihood was present, if somebody was present and the logic tells me that somebody should have been present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to deal, please, with some of the members of the SDS in Bosanski Petrovac. First of all, we've dealt with Mr. Novakovic. Was he the President of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was he also a member of the municipal board of the SDS in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: He was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was the President of that municipal board somebody called Dragan Ivanic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there also a Mr. Bogdan Latinovic, who was both a member of the assembly, the republican assembly, and a member of the SDS board in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Mr. Latinovic was a member of the municipal board. I think he was one of the so-called delegated members. He was the President of the municipal board -- of the executive board, excuse me, of the municipality. But basically he wasn't a particularly strong partyman. He was there as a professional, rather.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We may come to some other people in a moment but you've told us you were the secretary to the executive board. Who was the secretary to the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Mr. Zarko Sikman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, theoretically, therefore, he should have been the person responsible for the secretarial duties at the assembly. Did you, however, from time to time, do administrative work for the assembly?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Mr. Sikman was, on the basis of the job description, he was to perform all the duties that had to do with the assembly, and in the early days of his tenure, he did do that. It particularly refers to the initial period, that is, 1991. However, even already at that time, at Mr. Novakovic's request, I took over some of the work, I started carrying out additional control supervision of various documents, especially the legal documents and I even started drafting those documents to be tabled and presented for discussion. And then my role began to grow and I was made responsible for an ever-larger number of things that had to be -- of documents that had to be prepared for the assembly so that by mid-1991, I took over the majority of those, how shall I call them, more important issues, at least in so far as legal regulations are concerned. Mr. Sikman had an additional responsibility, because he had continued to -- he continued to act as a secretary in the -- of the company that he used to work for before the war, that is he was there, a lawyer there, even though that was informal and he also was involved in some private business at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: So that I can really say that he, up to a point, misused his office and dodged work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, Mr. Novakovic, was he also on the main board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How influential a politician was Mr. Novakovic? I mean what were his contacts with the leadership like?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: My impression was that Mr. Novakovic was a very influential man, or rather he was what one usually calls a leader. Formally speaking, he didn't hold a particularly high-ranking office in the area but basically, in view of his natural traits, the skill with which he knew how to impose his authority, to establish a direct contact with people, to make them respect him, he was in point of fact a leader. He directly communicated with the republican leadership, both the joint one until it all caved in, and the leadership which represented the Serbs in the then B and H. For instance, I was present on several occasions when he would, without any formalities, but he would call -- but he would dial the numbers of the then members of the Presidency, Mrs. Plavsic and likewise with Mr. Radovan Karadzic, without any ado or anything, and as far as I gathered, he communicated with them as his peers. There were no particular formal -- he didn't use any particularly formal forms of address when he spoke with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to have a look, please, on this topic at P1826.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour this was referred to in the statement at page 4. Not the interview, the actual statement, the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is addressed to the assembly of the Republic of Serbia and the president of the Republic of Serbia, and it calls on both to "undertake all necessary measures in accordance with your constitutional obligations towards the Serbian people as a whole to protect the Serbian people in Croatia, on the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, on the state terrorism imposed by the Croatian leadership and the MUP. "Furthermore we ask you to provide the necessary weapons to arm people so that unprotected Serbian people, which was attacked during the Easter holiday of peace and love can be defended. We think it is necessary for the representatives of the Republic of Serbia to start participating in the works of all the organs on the Autonomous Region of Krajina and to establish to what extent the survival of the Serbian people has been threatened on its own territory." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And it goes on like that. And then at the bottom again, it's a signature and it's typed Mr. Novakovic. Again, can you identify the signature as that of Mr. Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise Mr. Novakovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you help us as to - there is no date on this - as to what this is referring to and why it was sent?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I can tell you that. It is true that this is not a formal letterhead. There is no date, there is no reference number or anything, and I suppose this was the omission of a clerk who did it because he did not follow the administrative procedure. Nevertheless, I think that the document is authentic. That is I know how the -- how things unfolded at the time when this document must have been written. There was an event which prompted such a document, and that was when the special units of the Croatian police tried to take over control in a part of Croatia's territory which had separated and become the SAO Krajina. Subsequently, this SAO Krajina proclaimed the Republic of Serb Krajina and that happened on the Orthodox Easter, which I think additionally upset the population and encouraged interethnic intolerance. And on that occasion, there were some armed skirmishes. As far as I can remember, on the -- on the Croat and on the both the Croat and the Serb side had one fatality each and several casual at this time. The Serbs were poorly armed even there. In our area apart from hunting weapons they had nothing and then Mr. Novakovic, referring to that particular incident, he practically calls upon those institutions in Serbia requesting that armaments be provided for the Serbs. Formally speaking, he is referring to a constitutional obligation which Serbia had introduced in its constitution, whether in 1990 or 1991, I believe it was done in 1990, which stipulated that it was Serbia's obligation to protect the interests of Serbs living in republics outside Serbia, and the last paragraph, the last passage, I think that this list of municipalities was his arbitrary decision to do that, because I do not think that he could have communicated with their presidents in such short a time. Besides, in Bihac, there was a Muslim majority and its president, its mayor, the municipal mayor, was a Muslim and I now recall his name. His name was Nenad Ibrahimpasic and I knew him personally. So that he couldn't have communicated with the municipal mayor, with the municipal president n Bihac and enlist his support for this activity. He could have done it with a Serb representative but that couldn't have been the municipal mayor. And then Sipovo, which is deep in the territory of B and H, in relation to Croatia, once again, I do not believe that he managed to communicate with them. Or that at that time they had any particular interest in the matter because Croatia was and is quite far away from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Two matters then. Does this relate to something that happened in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the immediate reason was the attempt by special police units of Republic of Croatia to put under their control the territory of the SAO Krajina, that is territories bordering on B and H.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And what we are talking about there, I think you've made that absolutely clear, is effectively the Croatian Krajina, what became the RSK?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And the last question on this: Do you know whether Mr. Novakovic had personal contact with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I think that for a period of time, perhaps before he was killed, perhaps it was in 1992, I know that he once tried to, thought to speak to Mr. Milosevic, or more to the point, that they went to look for flour, but whether Milosevic received him then or not, I am not sure but I know that he sought an audience with him and that a man was engaged there, he was the director of the commodity reserves in Serbia and it was through him that he sought an audience with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Don't worry, that's all I need. Thank you very much. You can hand that document back to the usher now. I want to move, then, please, to the autumn really of 1991. Did the war in Croatia increase the interethnic tensions in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. Up to a point. Not much but a little, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As a result of mobilisation, did armed men, armed members of the forces, start to arrive in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. After there was a change in the military organisation, I think the Knin Corps was formed, perhaps it existed from before, I don't know. Then a part of the Petrovac military conscripts in accordance with the plan which existed in the former Yugoslavia, was mobilised as part of the reserves into units which were in operative use in Croatia, on their arrival for a holiday these people brought back weapons with them very often, sometimes they brought up -- brought back weapons which were permitted, but they also brought back trophies from the front and this caused certain tensions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to show you two documents from October of 1991, please. First of all, one that's already been produced as P22 and then there is a new document, Your Honour, which is on the list, which has the disclosure number 2.572. Both of which documents, Judge, you've seen before. Now, the first document, P22, is a telex headed from -- it says "please deliver the telex to the president of the municipal assembly," and it's an order of the SDS party in Sarajevo which was made public at the meeting of all the municipal presidents on the 26th of October, 1991 in Banja Luka chaired by Mr. Karadzic and fully accepted at the session of the Presidency of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And first of all, sir, you were shown this when you were interviewed but have you seen -- had you seen this before the interview?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I don't think that I did, but I said in the interview that the form of the document, the way it looks, the way it's been executed and the incoming stamp, all of these things indicate that this is an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's headed to all the municipalities or the - sorry - municipal assemblies. How would it have come to you, to you in Petrovac, I mean, not you personally? By telex?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: The way the document looks, there is no doubt that it arrived by telex through the communications centre and the communications centre is an institution which was in each municipality before the war. It was used for special communications, and particularly in the event of war. So that it arrived through the communications centre by telex.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the document before that, if you can just look at that, is again it looks like some kind of -- I don't know, telex, maybe? And it's dated the 18th of October. That's handwritten. And it says, "I pronounce by the authority granted by the statute, the state of emergency in the SDS, binding for all SDS organs, members and personnel in the party authorities. "You will be receiving instructions --" I'm sorry. I thought you had been handed it at the same time. But can you keep -- don't give the other document back for the moment. "You will be receiving instructions about the measures daily," and so on and so forth. Had you seen this before you were shown it in the interview?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I didn't see this even during the interview with you. This is the first time that I see this document, the document bears a stamp by the -- of the Zavidovici municipality which is in central Bosnia, but I recall that a similar decision about the so-called suspension of political functions of the Serbian Democratic Party was adopted, I don't know in which period, probably when the war broke out or immediately prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What number are we going to give this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are on 2450.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This says that I pronounce by the authority granted by the statute, the state of emergency in the SDS binding for all SDS organs. Were the decisions made by Mr. Karadzic and members of the main board binding, as is stated here, on the municipal boards?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I have to say that this formulation, by the authority granted by the statute, does not mean anything, and means a lot. It means that in my opinion, at that point, there is no specific decree for the suspension or for the war operations, but in view of the authority of the President of the party, Dr. Karadzic, and in view of the circumstances which in some municipalities were extraordinary, I believe that these instructions were being implemented, the instructions that were coming, but for the most part, these instructions were implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is a slight difference. If the main -- leaving aside this particular document, if the main board issued instructions to the municipal board, were they obliged -- was the municipal board obliged to carry out unless for some reason it was impossible, an instruction could not be carried out? As a general principle, I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: The general principle was to carry out those decisions, and this was done, except in special cases which perhaps we'll discuss later, in cases where it was impossible to carry them out, when, from a technical point of view, or a legal point of view, it was not possible to carry them out or it was not sensible to do it, but generally they were respected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you have back for a moment the instructions of the 29th of October, which was signed by Mr. Brdjanin as the vice-president of the assembly of the autonomous region? Can you tell us which of these instructions were implemented in Petrovac? For example, the "instruction number 1, a command of the town and round-the-clock duty."

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: The majority of these instructions were never carried out in Petrovac. Some of these orders are illegal, and unconstitutional. For example, order number 1 was never carried out, and the military command even much later, much later, requested for a command of the town to be set up. I personally told President Novakovic at the time if this were to happen that I would be the first to find a way to escape from Petrovac, and that we would all be in danger if a military command were to be formed, if there were to be a town command to be formed. A command of the town is a military occupational institution. It's not a representative of any kind of civilian authority. So that item number 1 was never carried out in Petrovac except for round-the-clock watch. This was not by the SDS. This was something that was done by the entire staff. I occasionally was on duty myself, if a meeting had to be held immediately, you will see based on documents that some meetings were held at night. It was not also in our authority to carry out full mobility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we -- I think if we cut this short because you dealt with this in the interview, in fact, was -- about the only one that was partially implemented was item number 7?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. That item was implemented then and also much later. This was something that was carried out continuously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: This referred to food supplies, clothing, medical supplies, medical service. This is something that was planned before in our municipality and was done even before the war, and during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So if we take this in the round, as I say, to try and cut this short, is it your position that almost nothing that was put into this order was carried out by Petrovac at this time, in October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: For the most part, none of this was implemented. There was no need in the municipality of Petrovac for any of these actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: At the time when this decision was adopted and when this instruction arrived, we were not in a position to have a serious number of deserters. Were anybody to leave the Knin Corps at the time, they would have to come back quickly. If they brought illegal equipment and weapons back and they concealed it and the police didn't have any indications of it being anywhere, making lists of surplus goods, even during the war, we traded on economic principles and continued production in our companies throughout the war, so we didn't give anything to anyone nor did we ask for anything from anybody. We did trade, of course. Paramilitary formations that are mentioned here, we didn't have any of those. The first such formations -- the first formations that appeared, appeared during mobilisations so this could refer to some of our neighbouring municipalities, some of these items.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, in order not to spend too much time on this, to summarise, these things that were being dealt with here were not causes for concern in your municipality at this stage, is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: It would be a fair summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can put that back or give it back to the usher. Now, I want to ask you about Mr. Brdjanin who signed that telex. Can you remember now when was the first time that you heard about Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I actually didn't really hear of him. The first time I saw Mr. Brdjanin was actually when I heard of him for the first time. On one occasion, on the instruction of the then-president, Mr. Novakovic, had something to do with the organisation of the court or the prosecutor's office in Petrovac and this is why I had to go to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll pause there because as we'll see that was clearly in 1992 because there is a record of your meeting. Before you went to Banja Luka in 1992, had you heard of Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We are going to look at a number of documents starting in around May of 1992, where there was communication between the autonomous region assembly and then Crisis Staff and your Crisis Staff. Were you aware that Mr. Brdjanin was the President of the Crisis Staff in Banja Luka, the regional Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. I was, but I don't remember when I found out about it. As political representatives of the Banja Luka region, I know a doctor who was the president of the SDS, and I know of another man, his name was Dr. Vukic. I met him personally. Then I also knew another president who was either before or after Vukic. He was the director of a rubber manufacturing plant. There was also Mr. Kupresanin. He was a more prominent figure from that region. Mr. Brdjanin, I actually found out about him in relation to this activity of president or the vice-president of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. I don't remember the first time I heard his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In that case, we'll deal with this when we look at the documentation about that. Now, can we talk for a moment, please, about the radio and the sort of programmes that went out on the radio and television? Did -- was there a transmitter in Ostrelj?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. There was a transmitter at Ostrelj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And had that been destroyed by Serbs in 1991? Or was that destroyed by Serbs in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: It was never officially established who destroyed it, but from talks in cafes, I know and I think that that is probably true, that a group of people in the late evening hours or early morning hours went there and destroyed the transmitter. They were drunk. They either destroyed -- smashed it up or burned it. And the result was that we lost our TV signal. After that, we had a kind of backup option, but mostly all signals were weak in our area. It was not possible to hear or see very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge, I appreciate that you are making every effort to go into detail in answering the questions that are put to you. However, if you can keep yourself or restrict yourself to a shorter answer, I think we will get over faster. The reason is that most of the events that you are telling us about, we've heard from other witnesses. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know whether Judge Taya would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: If the group who destroyed the transmitter is Serb or not, he has not yet answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what I heard, it was a Serb group.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just, the simple point is, does that mean that after that, Petrovac could not receive the programmes from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: For a brief period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How long -- when you say a brief period, for how long?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, a month or two months or three months, possibly. I'm not sure. I know that an auxiliary transmitter was set up later. It was called Macja Greda or Ilijina Greda, I think. And this enabled us to receive the signals, but the signals were much weaker.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. At this stage, at the end of 1991, was Radio Petrovac still made up of different nationalities of reporters and management staff?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Radio Petrovac was a small station and it had perhaps one or two employees. I think that they were Serbs. I'm not sure. Later, more people were employed, after the war started, and all of those people were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look, please, at something from the radio station, P1817. Now, this is a document I think you had a chance to look at yesterday, or the day before. It's a news report apparently about the arrangements for the plebiscite that was to be held of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. If we look at the second paragraph, it says the opposition parties cannot and will not prevent their members from taking part in the plebiscite because as they said it's not right to forbid anyone from expressing their personal freedom. They are concerned by the existence of ballot papers in different colours which leads in advance to division. Was it the situation, sir, that the -- there were different coloured ballot papers for the Serbs and for those who were non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I don't believe that that could be the case. It's possible that the ballots were of different colours, and it's possible that there were different colours for yes and for no, but simply because of my work, I didn't have time to go to the plebiscite, even though I intended to do so, so I don't know what this is all about. I don't know if they are talking about the political colours, I don't know. But the way the news item is published, I think it's an authentic piece of news because the positions of the parties according to my recollection were faithfully and correctly conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Just finally on this, the last part, "The most important thing in this is that after reconciling positions concerning the plebiscite following the joint meeting, people went for a coffee together in the way that we in Bosanski Petrovac have become accustomed to doing." That seems to suggest that there was -- that even though there was political difference, the parties were able to socialise together, the SDA, the HDZ and the SDS or the SDS and the SDA. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. I agree, because interpersonal relations between the deputies, regardless of party affiliations were similar to what they were before. They would argue in the assembly, but during the breaks they would be together.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, you can put that away. Now can we deal, please, with the political developments between October and December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, maybe that -- I think it's probably -- I'm going to deal with a collection of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Judge, we will have a 25-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you have, please, P1814?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm on page 19 of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, this is a document dated the 24th of October, 1991. So effectively it's between the instructions from Karadzic and the telex that we looked at, which states that "after a debate at the session of the municipal board of the SDS, the following conclusion was adopted by a majority, namely to form a Crisis Staff of the assembly of the Bosanski Petrovac municipality." This hasn't got a signature. Would that suggest, sir, that this is a file copy?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: There is no signature, and I think not, because it is a filed copy because according to our administrative rules, it should have been signed too. That copy should have been signed too but I think that this was done by the then-SDS secretary, who had a law education but he wasn't very tidy, and presumably that is why the signature is lacking. I now recall that at that time, that is late 1991, Stevo Radosevic was the President of the SDS rather than Ivanic. Radosevic left that office I think because he was a private businessman, and this particular duty interfered with his business. But I still think that this is an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I just ask you this, and perhaps you can answer yes or no? Were you present at this session of the municipal board?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I don't remember, but as a rule, I attended those sessions, so I believe I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. It says that there is to be a Crisis Staff set up of the assembly but it's a decision being made by the SDS municipal board. If there was to be a Crisis Staff set up, should that not have been the decision of all the assembly, including the SDA members and any other members?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Your conclusion regarding the composition is correct in principle, but this staff must have been formed following the SDS instructions that we saw in those -- in that earlier document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. All right, can we just move, then -- you can hand that document back. Could we look at two other documents, please, for -- around the same period, P1815 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should add that this was a document that an objection was taken to by Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't want to trouble too much with the contents. Effectively it's dealing with the mobilisation, I think, and the formation of the 19th Partisan Brigade and says that Bosanski Petrovac will mobilise one battalion. Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I do. It is the signature of Jovica Sepa. At the time, he was the head of general administrative affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And the stamp on the top, what does that suggest to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: The stamp is, in point of fact, a reference mark but it is incomplete, and I suppose once again it is the omission of a clerk responsible because we do not see the reference number here either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. And now could you look at the next document, P1816? I'm sorry, forgive me, I ought to give that back to you a moment. It's dated the 5th of November, P1815. When we looked at the telex, we saw that there were some instructions about mobilisation. That was dated the 29th of October and this document is dated the 5th of November. Were the two of these -- was this order connected to the instructions in the telex?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. I would say so, bearing in mind the chronology, the chronological order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because it talks about establishing full mobility of the Territorial Defence and forming units. Thank you. Yes, I'm sorry, now could you have P1816, please? Which is dated the 2nd of November, so it's three days before this. And it's a news item about what is described as a public forum being held. And there we see in the second paragraph, "The secretary of the secretariat for general administration, Mr. Sepa, stated that four mobilisations had already been carried out in the area of Petrovac." We see that various members of the JNA were there. Milutin Vukelic and Colonel Selak. And somebody has crossed that out and written Osman Selak. Who was Milan Skundric?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Milan Skundric is a colonel, commander of the logistics base of the 5th Army District which before the war covered the republics of Slovenia and Croatia, and later on, when the base -- after the base had moved its materiel and after it pulled out from Croatia and Slovenia then they set up their logistics base in the area of Petrovac, and subsequently it moved to Banja Luka. And he was always the commander of that -- of that base. It's a logistics base responsible for the supply of ammunition, foodstuffs, medical supplies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. On the same topic of mobilisation, could you look at, please, Exhibit P1818, which is from the Territorial Defence staff of Petrovac and is a request for the issuing of effectively missing equipment? It states, in the second or third paragraph, that "since the JNA units from Croatia have been transferred into the area of our zone of operations," I think that's what that means, "we believe we are obliged to ensure mutual cooperation." Then it talks about the reorganisation of the Bosanski Petrovac Territorial Defence has increased the strength from 540 conscripts to 1700 and so and they are missing a number of items of weaponry, as we can see. So by December of 1991, there had been a huge increase, had there, in the number of men being mobilised?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: That's right. Except that they were not mobilised then. They were -- the files, the records were simply expanded and they were mobilised later, but once again it was the JNA which was on top of it. There was a complete battalion, infantry was mobilised, and that is 121 soldier and officer, I remember the figure exactly. And here they are asking to do this in order to expand the records, that is, the TO commander is trying to get the weapons from the then command on the strength of this and that was still the JNA command which had moved to the BH territory from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I want to ask you, please, a little bit at this stage about the acquiring of weapons by the Serb population. By this stage in 1991, was any pressure being brought upon President Novakovic to arm the persons of Serbian nationality?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. The pressure was exercised on different occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How did you find out about it? Did he tell you about it or were you present when some of these -- this pressure was brought to bear?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: As a rule, I was present when such groups of people came. As a rule he did not speak to me about that except perhaps because of those visits he would do it later on, because his view was that people should know only what their immediate business was, but I saw these groups come. They were, to all intents and purposes, informal delegations from what was called neighbourhood communities, so these would be local organisational units from different areas, several villages would make for one neighbourhood community, and one would have the representatives of citizens, they would put together delegations, four, five men strong. And they invariably came with slightly panicky requests that they be provided with weapons, that they were under threat, that they were in great peril, and the president resisted those pressures thinking that they were exaggerating things, and that they were basically trying to come by weapons, which could then lead to trouble because they were neither army units nor was there any way to keep those citizens under any kind of control. And that was in 1992, I think it was January, after the mobilisation, such pressures ceased completely. I mean he simply refused to see any more such delegations, because by that time, some people had refused to take up even those army weapons, that is they refused to subject themselves to the military command, so that these requests remained merely on paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, in 1992, after the mobilisation, did Serbs respond to the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes, by and large, but there was also a certain number of Muslims who responded too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And those who responded to mobilisation, would they be given weapons automatically?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: They got them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before that, though, when these people were coming to see Mr. Novakovic, these communities, did they say anything to Mr. Novakovic about what was happening in other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. They said how other municipalities had allegedly already procured weapons, that they had allegedly already formed some detachment and that was it. We are lagging behind. And he kept saying that we were not in danger -- in any danger because we are too far from the theatres of operations and I know that he checked it with other municipalities. I know that he called their leaders and once he told me personally as I was trying to draft a document, that he had found out that they were lying. So it was thought that they were trying to somehow lay their hands on weapons and then use them at their own discretion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think again just to complete this, is it right that you discovered, or it was discovered, that weapons had been smuggled in particular from a place called Kragujevac?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you discover that weapons had been smuggled from there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: It wasn't I who discovered it. I learned it through informal conversations with people, that hunting carbines were being offered and they allegedly had been brought from Kragujevac, that they were new carbines, Remington carbines, and in a pub, in a tavern or somewhere, one of men said, "well, if you want to, we can get it for you and it's 1.000 German marks." I said I didn't want it, that my husband had a hunting weapon at home.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "That my father," excuse me, "had a hunting weapon at home."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just answer the question so that we move along because we are expecting a long cross-examination so we need to move along as speedily as we can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can we have a look -- could you please be shown, please, this is the last part of December, 1991, Exhibit P1819? And at the same time, could you also be given, please, P25? Now, if you look first of all at P1819, this is a meeting of the SDS party secretariat on the 26th of December, 1991, and it's the minutes, apparently this was the first meeting. You apparently were present. And if you look at item 2, the instruction on the organisation and activity of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in emergency circumstances needs to be typed in seven copies and every member of the Secretariat is to be given a copy. This was to be organised and carried out by Nenad Dragicic [phoen]. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: He was the party secretary at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at -- if you look just briefly at P25, that's the document headed, "Instructions for the organisation and activity," et cetera. Do you remember these instructions being discussed at this meeting on the 26th of December?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: According to the contents of the minutes, I believe so, but it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: But yes, that is -- how it should have been in the regular course of events.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, it said that there was to be seven copies for every member of the secretariat. Do you remember being given a copy?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but quite possibly, I suppose I was. And if I was present at the meeting, I would simply put such documents in a drawer or something. I didn't study them particularly. I mean, in view of the job and my responsibilities, that was really a secondary activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you look at just the last page? There is a stamp on it and a signature. Do you recognise the signature? I'm sorry, not of -- I'm sorry of Exhibit P1819, I'm so sorry, not the actual instructions.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: The stamp is of the Serb Democratic Party. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And the signature?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I believe it to be authentic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The instructions in there, we went through them in the interview, but did you -- you came under, I think, the Variant A type of municipality because you were a municipality where the Serbs were in the majority. Did you follow those instructions? For example, around-the-clock staffing?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes, regular standing duty for a while. Later on, it was not necessary and so it stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then, "daily meetings of the secretariat so that the situation on the ground can be constantly monitored and evaluated." Were there daily meetings, that you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: No, no. It wasn't possible technically so that was one reason, and there was no need for that. They met when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then the SDS municipal board shall immediately form a Crisis Staff. You had in fact rather pre-empted that, hadn't you, because you did that in October, or at least you laid the groundwork?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. We did positively because some instructions were conveyed verbally and now I cannot remember, but there is no doubt that some instructions were verbal and that formal documents would be drawn up subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have done this document to death by now as I know Your Honours will recall earlier on in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, can we move, please, into 1992? And let us now deal with a document that you actually were responsible for. Could you be shown, please, the copy of your notebook or diary?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think a page was provisionally exhibited by Ms. Sutherland. Do you remember there was some discussion about this and I don't know whether she informs me it was given some sort of provisional number. I think it came up during the course of Mr. Treanor's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What you're suggesting, Ms. Korner, I have a recollection of, but I would rather not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ms. Gustin is going to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would rather not confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it will help because it was given a provisional number so if we stick to the same number then it's easily -- although it's out of sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I certainly do recollect Ms. Sutherland making use of one page of someone's notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I wouldn't say it was this witness's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was, and we will come to the page she asked Mr. Treanor about. It was given a provisional number of P2369. And it seems to me that the whole -- if the whole diary becomes that one exhibit number, then it's easy to connect the two up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was put in on the 3rd of July, as I say with Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have the transcript of the 3rd of July on --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We were sitting in another courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right. But I think Ms. Gustin confirms that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do not put it in doubt, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The page, I think, that was referred to was the one for the 14th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. And I'm going to go back to that one now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I recall, I think Your Honour said that it would be admitted once it was proved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, is that a copy of a diary or notebook that you kept during the period 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened to that notebook when you left Petrovac in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: It stayed in my desk.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In your desk, what, in the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you've had an opportunity to go through this before. Do you confirm that that is in your writing and it is a photocopy of your document?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. I confirm its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want you to turn, please, in that notebook to the 14th of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is on page 26 of our translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On that date, did you record the -- first of all there was an executive board meeting it looks like and then an SDS Serb Democratic Party assembly in Sarajevo at 1745 that day? And is it clear that you attended that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I attended one assembly session in Sarajevo, instead of President Novakovic. He sent me but I think this was during the declaration of the Serbian assembly or the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's possible that -- it's possible that these are the conclusions which were brought over from that assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember -- but do you remember -- I think you told us this before -- that you attended a session -- some meeting in the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo? While Mr. Novakovic was in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was the Holiday Inn or the B and H assembly. I'm not sure. I know I passed through checks at the entrance and then speeches were given, Dr. Karadzic was present. I don't know whether that was on this same day or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: But I was there on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, what you're recording here, it's been translated as entry speech, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, and it's the first part that I'm interested in, it says -- I'm sorry, could you just read because the translator had difficulty in reading your writing here. Could you just read what you say after that first sentence after Dr. Radovan Karadzic? Could you just read it aloud?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I will read it out aloud and I can also interpret it. "Activate the second degree, activate organs of authority so that they practically carry out their duties."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know what that was referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: With -- by "activating the second degree," what they mean is according to what I recollect from the instructions on the division of the municipalities into the A and B categories, I think the second degree or level is a higher level of alert and readiness, and "to activate the organs of authority to practically carry out their duties," this probably refers to the group of the B type where the Serbs did not have a majority so these organs of theirs, which had separated, needed to actually function and perform as an administration or an administrative service for the citizens because up until that point they were just formally organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Then apparently he talked about the referendum, said the Serbs must not take part in it, because they've already given their declaration on this matter. Was that a reference, I think it's fairly obvious, to the up-and-coming referendum on independence for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then the final part, under -- the one before the bottom of that page, strategic goal to uphold Serbia and Montenegro and necessary support for our -- could you just -- I'm sorry, could you read that sentence as well because again there was difficulty, where it starts, strategic goal?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: "Strategic goals, to preserve Serbia and Montenegro, a necessary mainstay or support for our goals."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. And then the next part, definition of the Serb people, or Bosnia-Herzegovina nationals. All right. Can I now deal, please, with what happened later on in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I just lost my place for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, please, P1822. This is a document apparently signed by Mr. Kerkez, the chief of police in Bosanski Petrovac, and it's a request to the army for weaponry and uniforms and the like. So it looks as though it goes along with the earlier document that we saw from the TO. Again, do you recognise -- did you know Mr. Kerkez?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
