utterances.text: I knew Mr. Kerkez. He has died.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Are you able to identify his signature?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I saw him infrequently but I think that the signature is authentic, in view of the way the document is written and in view of the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you aware that the Petrovac police were seeking further uniforms and weaponry?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. It did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Ah, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I'm reminded by Ms. Gustin this was one of the other documents that Mr. Ackerman objected to and you reserved judgement until we identified it. So -- in fact, I think identified its source. Just let me check that. I think we did identify a source eventually but I thought -- this is P1822. Yes. Your Honour, this was one we did identify. It took a long time but I think you reserved judgement on it just so you're aware of it. Thank you. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we move, please, to 1824? The 11th of March. Now, in summary, this is a member of the Crisis Staff, the Serbian People's Crisis Staff, held on the 11th of March. You were present and the discussion resolved around who was going to be the commander of the public security station, and it appears that a Muslim, Fuad Ferizovic, had been appointed commander and there was some problem about this. Do you remember this discussion about who was going to be at the police station?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you -- very briefly in summary what was the problem?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: According to the interparty agreement at the level of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the parties in power had agreed amongst other things in those municipalities where one ethnic group was in a majority, to have the chief of police come from the ranks of that ethnic group, which was the most numerous, and the rest of the staff would be determined according to the ethnic key. In this case, the security centre in Bihac decided that a Muslim should be the chief in Petrovac, who was not actually accepted by that community. He was a Muslim. And he didn't have any experience in police work before that. So that is when this dissatisfaction began to appear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So even though, theoretically, about a year before, a decision had been taken to join the Banja Luka region, by the assembly, the Bihac region was still attempting to exercise authority in Petrovac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: It's correct, and we continued to work with them still.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you have a look, please, now, at the P1825? This is a document that you saw, I think, yesterday. Again, can you identify, it's a very bad copy, but does that look like Mr. Novakovic's signature?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to deal at this stage --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour this is at page 3 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- with this question of instructions and requests. Under the conclusions on the first of April, 1992, we see that Bosanski Petrovac citizens are requested to refrain from disorderly conduct. Under item number 7, first of all item number 6, the Territorial Defence staff is instructed to issue an order to the territorial units to assume control of the territory and under item 7, the public security station in Bosanski Petrovac is instructed to ensure total control of passage and entry into the Bosanski Petrovac of all persons. Now, was there a difference between a request, as phrased, and an instruction?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. There is a difference. If you use the term "are instructed, are ordered" it means that it's an order. But if you use some other term, such as "are called upon to" then it's more of a recommendation and a request that does not essentially have to be carried out. But when it is said here, "are instructed to," then it means that it's an order, even though the expression "are instructed to" is used as a rule when the organ that issued it does not have any legal grounds to issue an order and is actually trying to appropriate more power than it enjoys under the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we deal with that? The order to the public -- there are a number of orders -- I'm sorry, instructions, or orders, to the public security station. I don't know whether you were actually familiar with either the Bosnia-Herzegovina law of the interior or the subsequent Republika Srpska, but in your view, what powers did the municipal assembly and the Crisis Staff have to order the police?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: In the formal sense, they did not have the authority or the powers. They could have expressed their dissatisfaction or they could give recommendations. As a rule, requests should have been carried out through a higher organ, the regional organ, first Bihac and then Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But here, as we can see, in number 7, it's saying it instructs, in number 9 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact -- if I may interrupt you, I would suggest you invite him to answer your question because he's only given a partial answer to it. I mean, he's told us what legally it should have been but was it so in practice? And since you were asked a question relating to both the municipal assembly and the Crisis Staff, may I ask you to keep them apart and tell us whether you perceived any difference between the Crisis Staff and the municipal assembly when it came to instructing or requesting the police or the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tried to explain that already, and I will try to complete my explanation as briefly as possible. These orders are a consequence, according to my understanding, of the existence of a law which was changed, perhaps a year before that, a law relating to internal affairs. According to a prior law, the municipality had direct powers over the local police. And all those people, the people in the municipality and in the police, by inertia, preserved their relations for the most part. As far as the assembly and the Crisis Staff are concerned, the Crisis Staffs were established as ad hoc bodies. The difference between the Crisis Staff and a municipal assembly is in the following: A Crisis Staff by its functions unified the legislative and the executive functions. It had the powers of the executive -- of the assembly and the executive board. That is why, directly by their functions, certain people had to be members of the Crisis Staff. A part of them or some of them were delegated from amongst experts and technically essential personnel. A further difference is in the following: Decisions adopted by the Crisis Staff had to be submitted for verification to the assembly later. Regardless of their ad hoc powers, they were a consequence of the current situation. The decisions of the Crisis Staff could be confirmed by the assembly, they could be changed or they could be cancelled. These are the differences, and if necessary, I can explain even further. In relation to the police, in a certain period, which was a transitional period, when the functions were being transferred from one regional centre to another regional centre, specifically from Bihac to Banja Luka, our police actually remained without any kind of real control from a regional centre, and it was effectively without a functional administration. The administration was never at a satisfactory level and it wasn't that particularly at that time. So in the functional sense, the assembly had augmented or higher powers over the police, and the police in essence, except for some key and dubious decisions, actually carried out instructions such as these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So if we can just summarise that, whatever the legal position may or may not have been, the reality was that the police did carry out some of the instructions of the assembly and the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just have a look, please, at Exhibit P202 on this topic, although this is jumping forward a little bit in time. This is a dispatch that was sent from the CSB in Banja Luka to all of the SJBs and its conclusions at -- of a meeting that was held on the 6th of May, which was attended by, it looks like, the chief of the Bosanski Petrovac SJB, amongst all the other municipalities. Can you look, please, at item number 14, first of all? Actually before you do that, until were you shown that document yesterday, had you ever seen it before? I should ask you that.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: The first time I saw it was when the investigator showed it to me, yesterday or the day before, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Item number 14, the chief of the CSB will arrange with the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina to make a decision entitling Banja Luka Security Services Centre to acquire all confiscated ownerless property, et cetera. As far as Petrovac was concerned, did the police confiscate what's described as ownerless property and use it to equip themselves? In particular, in respect of motor vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: The police could not do this, as far as vehicles are concerned, no confiscation was done but a mobilisation was carried out, so that vehicles which were mobilised in accordance with regular procedure were given to the police for their use. Besides that, I know of one case where one vehicle later than this period, was determined to have been stolen, and I think that the owner was from Bosansko Gravoho so this stolen vehicle was used.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then if you go, now, please to 23: "In all our activities, we are obliged to observe all measures and apply all procedures ordered by the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region." Is that something that surprises you as a decision taken?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I apologise. I cannot see item 23. In my copy I only go up to item 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may be on the other page. I think it's on the next page?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Ah, there is something on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. It should be on a separate page. Item 23, I think you saw that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you expect the CSB, and other police stations, to observe all measures and apply all procedures ordered by the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is a significantly different relationship than the one at the local police station level, because here there was, formally, a government of the region in existence, and by that logic, the police was obliged to abide by instructions so that this conclusion of theirs is in accordance with the regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then under that we see a reference to this disarmament deadline expiring on the 11th of May; "we should take no action until the Crisis Staff makes the relevant decisions and it's important we solve this problem comprehensively." And we will look at that when we come to the disarmament in Petrovac. Yes, thank you very much, sir, you can give that back to the usher. All right. Could you have a look, please, now, at Exhibit P153? This is a document addressed to the governments of the autonomous regions, the autonomous districts, of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to all Serbian municipalities, and it's dated the 16th of April and it says, "a state of an imminent threat of war is declared. General public mobilisation of the TO in the entire territory is ordered" and so on and so forth, and it's signed by Mr. Subotic. Did you see this document? I mean, I know you saw it in the interview, but had you seen it at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I think that I did, and based on the contents, I think that I did look at the document, and I'm saying this because I know that by referring to this legal grounds, at a later occasion I told the then-chief of cabinet of Dr. Karadzic that his legal basis was wrong, and that this Article 81 does not give the powers or the authority for these actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But nonetheless, by -- what effect did that have in Petrovac? Did you start to mobilise? Is that the mobilisation that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: It did not affect the municipality of Petrovac in no way, because the mobilisation had already been completed by that time, on -- at that day, more people had been mobilised in Bosanski Petrovac than the military rules allowed even.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you look, please, next at Exhibit P157, same month, April? 26th of April this time. That's an excerpt from the instructions for the work of the municipal Crisis Staffs of the Serbian people signed by the Prime Minister, Mr. Djeric. Do you recall receiving that document?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Not exactly, but this document must have been used, no doubt, because the instruction, the instruction under item 2 confirms what I've just said, that certain members had been appointed ex officio and some other items too, I don't want to go into that, but this is an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And in number -- item number 14, the last item, the Crisis Staff shall convene and make decisions in the presence of all its members, take official minutes, issue written decisions, and submit weekly reports to the regional and state organisations of the Serbian republic. I think we'll see some of the reports that you sent to the region. Do you remember if you did weekly reports or just occasional reports?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. Possibly that initially at the time when the instructions were issued, the reports were weekly, and I guess that later on, they were submitted now and then, and then eventually ceased to be ceased [as interpreted] because the organisation was changed by then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you. You can give that document back now. Thank you very much. I want to move, then, for a moment to your notebook. Can you -- we're really -- yes, if we just look for a moment please at your entry for the 6th of April, our page 47, we see -- there is a -- there is a -- I suppose you could call it a shopping list, but "cigarettes, (400 packets)" but then: "Fax 39-155 (Banja Luka) Serbian Democratic Party Secretariat request for replacement of Chief of Public Security Station." Does that relate back to what we saw being discussed in that executive -- in the Secretariat minutes?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: No. No. It doesn't. Here, the replacement of Chief Kerkez was being sought, because Chief Ferizovic never took up the office. I forgot to tell you that. And President Novakovic was not on good terms with Kerkez, and never stopped asking for his removal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So eventually, as we will see, was he removed and replaced by Mr. Gacesa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Gacesa is the one who took up the job that was earmarked for Fuad Ferizovic but the witness can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just clarify, sir? Who became the chief of the public security station?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: The chief of the SJB, Fuad -- well, Fuad Ferizovic never became chief. After the opposition to his appointment by the Serbs, nobody even tried to bring him into the office. So that Kerkez was succeeded by Gacesa. I'm not sure whether Kerkez was dismissed and then appointed an inspector or was it the illness which made him leave because I know that he died at an early age.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Then if we just very quickly move through your diary for the beginning of May, 7th of May, page 48, Your Honours, you apparently went to Banja Luka, and had conversations there about -- it was really schooling, was it, education generally?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Let me see, yes, correct, correct. If you want me, I'll clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I don't think we need it but just to note that you were apparently told to contact Mr. Erceg and we can see that on page 50 who was going to become -- who was going to announce who the Minister of Education for the Autonomous Region of Krajina was going to be. Mr. Koljevic, apparently -- Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I was to establish contact with Mr. Erceg because we were about to found a secondary school. The secondary school in Bosanski Petrovac had been abolished a long time before that. We were trying to reinstate one. And that was why I wanted to see him, and at that time I also communicated with the then head of the teaching administration regarding the necessary personnel and their structure, the kind of teachers that we would need.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, staying with your diary, please, then, can we go to your entry for the 9th of May, 1992, where there was a meeting with the SDA? And you've recorded, have you, a Mr. Hidic speaking. Could you just tell the Court who Mr. Hidic was, the first name of Mr. Hidic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic -- everybody knew Mr. Hidic as Sasa but his real name is Safet and he was a member of parliament from Petrovac, and he was representing the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And what he's -- he's talking about there is the reserve military units, violent behaviour, threats made by other citizens, reservists shooting and expressed the willingness of the Muslims to puts on uniforms and defends the borders of the Petrovac municipality but not against other Muslims and they refused to go anywhere else. First of all, was this a bone of contention between the Serbs and the Muslims that they were refusing to answer the mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. It was a bone of contention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the other matters that he's talking about, the threats and the behaviour in cafes and reservists shooting, by May, was there already a problem of violence against the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Well, the problem of violence emerged when a larger number of soldiers turned up. That is as far as I can remember, it was precisely at that time, in early May, when a sizeable number of soldiers came on leave from different units and from the different fronts. As a rule, soldiers returned with weapons they had been issued with, and the military were not sufficiently well organised so that the commands could not keep them under control. The municipal authorities requested on various occasions that this control be established, and Mr. Hidic is insisting on this, because Muslims and the number of them who reported to those units was insignificant, these Muslims feared all this shooting around town, and they feared people who would get drunk and then use wantonly very serious weapons. Then he talks about threats coming from some citizens which practically means that one of those armed soldiers, and presumably some civilians too, threatened citizens of Muslim ethnicity which indicates that the Muslim community in Petrovac was concerned and through their member of parliament, Hidic, wished to convey that concern to the Serb authorities. Dismissals, well, a certain number of individuals in companies and public services were fired because they had failed to respond to call-up summons, and the wives of such individuals were also given notice. However, it affected mostly the Muslims because they, by and large, did not respond. As for the Serbs, I know that in one or two cases, wives were dismissed from their jobs because their husbands had evaded mobilisation. And this readiness expressed here for the Muslims to put on, to put on uniforms, it went on even after this period of time, but there was really a moral problem with the Muslims putting on the uniforms of the Serb troops and going out to the front to confront the Muslim -- other Muslims. So some of them agreed to go to the front in Livno.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And if we just turn over our page, it may be on the bottom of your own, but you've written: "The issue of weapons owned by Muslims should also be considered." What was that referring to, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's at page 53, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a general wording, and it could mean two things. One, and perhaps more likely one, is that it deals with the legal weapons owned by Muslims, because there were hunters, sportsmen and the like, mostly as hunters. Or to protect their property. So those would be mostly pistols or revolvers, so I guess that it is that kind of weapons that is meant here. And possibly, also, the Muslims had managed to come by some of the formation, some of the proper army weapons, and perhaps any weapons owned by Muslims are meant here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then can we look, please, yes, before we look at the 12th of May meeting in your diary, could you look, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I did miss this out on my list as well, I would just ask it to be put on the ELMO. P186. It's in the Petrovac binder after divider 21. If we just put the English on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were shown this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he was shown this in the interview. It's at page 39 of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is addressed to the president of the municipal assembly dated the 11th of May, pursuant to the decision of the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region of the 11th of May, we submit to you the statement of accounts. Now, at the same time, you will need Exhibit 227, please. Actually, in fact, I'm sorry, we don't have that particular conclusion. No, we don't, regrettably. Of course this is not a complete list of all the conclusion. Anyhow, it says, "Could you please immediately -- if you go back to P186, could you please immediately deposit the said amounts to transfer the amounts? And we see on their Bosanski Petrovac was supposed to be paying 15.552 dinars -- no, sorry, it was 15.000 population times 30 dinars, 466.000?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: That's the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you paid this amount or anything like this?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I wasn't responsible for the implementation of national decisions. It was the administrative affairs department, but we complied with all our duties, so I presume we did pay this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And can you now have, please, Exhibit 1828, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That is on my list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, this is addressed, it's dated the 10th of May, addressed to the Autonomous Region of Krajina, the war staff, Banja Luka, report on the conduct of mobilisation, and it's signed on behalf of, I think, Za, president of the National Security Council, Mr. Novakovic. So Mr. Novakovic was the President of the assembly and the president of the National Security Council, was he?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: That's right. And he was also the President of the Crisis Staff, ex officio.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I wrote this document and it was with his authorisation, I also signed it and sent it. I suppose that it was a formal letter, and it did not require a special procedure. We merely point in it at a problem of an excessive number of people being mobilised and that it is becoming an economic threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: And perhaps, sorry, I also see that we are letting them no that the cooperation with JNA has been put in place or rather that the TO units had been placed under the JNA command. In other words, we did not have any territorial or local units, we never had them under our control. They were always part of the official formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you. Now, can we for a moment, please, go back to your diary? First of all, the 11th of May?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Our page 56, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It starts with something to do with the transmitter, but underneath that, you've noted the name Ciganovic and in brackets, (N. Sad). Was that -- who was that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Mr. Ciganovic was originally from Petrovac. I think he worked in the police or in some security service or something. I met him. We were introduced but I never tried to find out what he really did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: But it was because of this local connections and because he had relations there, he was supposed to try to find a transmitter so that our radio could start working again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember what his first name was?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I don't know, because I was a newcomer to Petrovac and those people who knew him had known him from before. He was about 50 years of age, perhaps 50 odd.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move then to the next day, the 12th of May, in your diary? And you had a meeting at 3.15 in the afternoon, clearly with representatives of the army and also it would appear with representatives from other municipalities including Mr. Klickovic from Krupa. I think was Mr. Vjestica there as well?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Well, my copy is pretty poor and I can't see his name but if his name does not figure here, then he wasn't there because I really took care to put -- to be very precise about who attended what meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And where was Mr. Kovacevic, Stevo Kovacevic, from?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I don't remember. You know, I came to meet people for the first time quite often. They would come ex officio, we would be introduced, but I didn't really know much about them, at least quite a number of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So from your municipality, you were there, was Rajko, President Novakovic, Bogdan, Mr. Latinovic, was Obrad Vrzina?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Let's see, from the Petrovac municipality, from the Petrovac municipality, there were Novakovic, then yes, Bogdan Latinovic, Obrad Vrzina, and I was there too. There was also the President of the assembly from Bihac, which I suppose was Ibrahimpasic, then municipality of Krupa, with associates, then General Spiro Nikovic, Miro Rokvic, must have been an officer, an army officer or something but now I remember, Savo Kovacevic with associates, Savo Kovacevic should have been one of the senior officer with the then JNA but he wasn't present since I crossed him out. I suppose I expected them to turn up because they had been announced and so, to be more efficient, I put their names in advance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To summarise, it looks there was a -- Mr. Klickovic started talking and talked about facts suggesting that the mujahedin were in Bosanska Krupa preparing criminal plans and General Nikovic or Ninkovic emphasised the necessity of the division of the Croat and Muslim territories, and measures for the return of officers to the Serbian republic. Now, were you aware that that day in Banja Luka there was an assembly meeting taking place, of the Serbian assembly?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: No. I wasn't aware of that, but on the other hand, I know what was discussed in detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: At the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were -- where was this meeting taking place? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: In the municipal hall, I believe. I mean that was the common practice. As a matter of fact, I'm quite sure that it was in the municipal hall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in this discussion, there is a lot of discussion about the Muslims and the like. Was -- were the Muslims regarded as a threat by the Serbs from Bihac and from Krupa?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: A minor correction, sorry, I said something which is not quite right. It transpires from the note that Dr. Stevo Beslac was the municipal mayor from Bihac, and not Nenad Ibrahimpasic, which in other words means that that municipality had already split along the ethnic lines. Now I'll answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. It's all right. Yes, were the Muslims in Krupa --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- And Bihac, did the Serbs, Mr. Klickovic, Mr. Beslac regard the Muslims as a threat?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: They did regard them as a threat. I think that this meeting took place after the fighting in Krupa, because it says that there was no plundering or rape during the combat but that now the looting had started, which is people who were plundering the Muslim property who -- which remained in this part of Krupa and that means that there was some combat operations during the meeting and that is why the representatives of the superior command were present there. But Serbs, as a population, not only these two leaders, but Serbs as such were very afraid of Muslims in that area because during World War II, at a place Stara Govedarica, some 7.500 Serbs were killed, at Crno Jezero 4.000 Serbs and in Bihac, at one site only now, there are different figures, some say 12.000, others 5 -- 15.000 Serbs, so because, they were a minority, they were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. I was going to say don't worry about the numbers in World War II but can you just answer this question, yes or no? In 1992, were people in Bihac, Krupa and Petrovac still remembering the events of World War II?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we break now? Okay. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honours, before Ms. Korner gets started, can I point out a possible error in transcription. And the witness, obviously, would need to confirm this. Page 37, line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, page 37?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I believe if I've got my passage identified correctly this deals with the number of men in a battalion. The transcription says 121, I believe he testified to 721.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcript it says infantry was -- "there was a complete battalion infantry was mobilised and that is 121 soldiers and officers. I remember the figure exactly." Did you say 121 or 721?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said 721. 721.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Cunningham. Thank you, Judge. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, just to finish off on that meeting, we were talking about how people in Bihac and Krupa regarded the Muslims as a threat. As far as Petrovac was concerned, there was -- in your view, was there any serious threat from the Muslims, given the number of Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: The Muslims who lived in Petrovac, in my opinion, did not pose a serious threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right, now on that day, that is the 12th of May, I think the assembly decided on the strategic goals and we will see the nexus between that and what was said in your meeting. Could you now be given disclosure 2.573.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, this is actually another translation of what is already P189, but it's a better translation. So it may be that we want to replace the translation, if nothing else but not make it a separate -- or we could simply make this P189.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's better.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the decision after the assembly held that day of what the strategic goals were and it's under -- it has the signature block or whatever, typed signature, of Momcilo Krajisnik. Do you remember hearing about this at the time that it was made, this decision? Because it was published in the gazette in November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: This decision was not heard of or known about in 1992. I saw this decision when it was published, and I think it was after the 26th of November, 1993. Certain decisions were made with a considerable delay, after a situation was established, then the decisions would be modified in accordance to what was wanted or in accordance to the actual situation on the ground and I think this is one of such decisions. For example, on the 12th of May, 1992, this corridor between Semberija and Krajina, I don't know whether it was in question at all or the corridor in the Drina River valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Don't worry because, in fact, we have the full record of the session, so we know these things were talked about. All I was asking you is whether you personally knew about it in 1992. And your answer, I gather, is you didn't?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But in your meeting, General Ninkovic was emphasising the necessity of the division of the Croat and Muslim territories. Did you understand him to be saying that was a division from the Serbian territories?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: General Ninkovic's intention at this meeting did not coincide with the intentions mentioned in this decision of the 12th of May, 1992. I am sure of that for the following reasons: General Ninkovic was a professional officer. He was known as a person who did not have any particular leanings towards national interests, and he wanted a division in the area of western Krajina. There was some discords in Krupa and Bihac. There was a compact Croat community in the area of Bihac, in several villages, and this is what he talked about. At the same time, accords were being made, parallel with this, between Mr. Ibrahimpasic as the President of Bihac, with some Serb representatives. I know about this personally because we went several times for negotiations and this was for a division to be made in the Bihac municipality in such a way that the Serbs would set up their own administration in a part of that municipality, and the Muslims would do the same in their part. This is what General Ninkovic meant. This is the division that he was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. First of all I think you refer to that, if you look at the end of your note, our page 58, where somebody says it's important that the Serbian Municipality of Bihac be quickly established. But in effect, you're saying that what General Ninkovic and other people at the meeting were talking about, if I've understood you correctly, is that the Serbian territories should separate from the Muslim and Croat?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's what was said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you look, please, then at the very end of your note, you've recorded there that -- this is our page 59 -- that -- in fact, it's a continuation, you say that would give us great advantages by establishing municipalities, "Serbs would attain almost everything they are entitled to. Militarily Serbs in Bihac have completely failed." Then underneath that, you have written a number and the name "Martic." Was that Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just to summarise that, that is the Milan Martic who is awaiting trial here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I don't think -- I hope there is not going to be any dispute about this, you told us about this in interview, was this in connection with you going to Dalmatia to collect fuel which was then seized by Martic, and you had to go and negotiate with Martic to get the fuel?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. This is fuel that our municipality bought and they prevented us from actually getting it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then you've also recorded the name of Milomir Stakic, the Prijedor municipal assembly. Was that you giving -- it says 100 tonnes of fuel, was that you obtaining fuel from Prijedor or providing fuel to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Regarding Stakic, they had 100 tonnes of fuel and of those 100 tonnes, we were to receive a certain quota which was to be divided amongst several municipalities. We were supposed to get the fuel. There is a military warehouse which was situated in that municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever meet Stakic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: No. I never met him, but on one occasion, I saw him at a meeting. I only had contacts with him about the fuel or with his staff, and I know that we did receive our entire quota.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you just tell us what meeting did you see him at, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: There was a meeting, I think at the Prijedor assembly or somewhere, but it was in Prijedor anyway. I don't remember in which building. President Novakovic sent me because he could not go. So I went to see what would be discussed and also to convey to him the information about the meeting. There was a large number of representatives from municipalities throughout the region. I also saw him on another occasion when he was passing through Petrovac. That time he was the President of the regional board of the Serbian Democratic Party because the party had been reorganised. And they were going to a meeting on the border with Croatia. They went to a tourist resort. And that's the other time that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Can you move now, please, in your diary or your notebook, to the 18th of May, which is page 64 of the English version? And just -- it's really the next page that -- for us, Your Honour, page 65 that I'm interested in. You've written in part of that entry, "consent" -- "Rajko, Presidency," and then, "consent on behalf of the Crisis Staff, request to the Krajina government for 25 tonnes." What was that about?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: It's hard to remember it all. The request to the government of Krajina for 25 tonnes is probably about securing fuel, because during that period, it was a problem to obtain fuel. I don't know about the Crisis Staff bit with the working president. It probably could mean that the Presidency of the Crisis Staff or the Presidency of the assembly needed to be organised. So this was just a note reminding me of a certain obligation that I had to carry out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, can we move, please, still on your diary, to the following day, the same page, 19th of May, there was a "Crisis Staff at 8.00 urgent". Does that mean there was a Crisis Staff meeting at 8.00?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I believe so, yes, and I have it in my notes, I also have the minutes by hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: And it's unfinished, but yes, this was a reminder to inform the members at 8.30, and this obligation was also for the day before, so I was obliged to inform them that the President instructed that a meeting should be convened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you go, please, to part of your notebook, it's on our page 66, where you have written, "I am exchanging an apartment in Bihac" and then you describe it, "Suitable for remodelling into business premises for the equivalent in Banja Luka. Offer should be made." Can you tell us, it was a personal thing or it was a draft for a general dealing with exchanges of property?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: It's possibly part of a general exchange of property. However, this was a specific case. This is my boss at the time, the President of the executive board, who instructed me to make the ad and to send it to a newspaper, probably to Banja Luka. Yes, Glas is the -- Glas newspaper of Banja Luka. And I did send this ad there. So he wanted to exchange his apartment, he wanted to exchange his apartment in Bihac for an apartment in Banja Luka. He did do that but then this decision was later cancelled by the High Representative after which he sold the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We will come on to this as a topic a bit later but at this stage, in May of 1992, was there already beginning the procedure whereby Muslims could exchange property with Serbs in Bihac or Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Possibly that something had begun but this was not very much. Only later did this become a mass occurrence, this exchange of property.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I missed out something that happened a little earlier. I'd like you to look, please, as Exhibit P1829. This is really dealing with disarmament. This is a meeting on the 15th of May of the Crisis Staff, again were you present and on this occasion actually taking the minutes?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I was present and I was taking the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if you look at the signature at the end, whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I've already looked. It's Mr. Novakovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to stop, the reason I'm doing this because all these documents were objected to by Mr. Ackerman. I'll stop if -- perhaps Mr. Cunningham can confirm before tomorrow that the objections are now dropped. Otherwise, I'm going to have to go on doing this throughout--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We understand what you're up to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's just wasting time if the objection is withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I cannot stop you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. What I mean, this is really where the Defence have to come forward and say we drop the objection. Otherwise I have to go on proving this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll inform the Court of that first thing in the morning, but my guess is the objection will remain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can do did in another matter. You can just bring all these documents out now, hand them one after the other to the witness, let him go through them, and then we'll just have a confirmation from him or a denial, one of the things, whether they are authentic or not, whether he has reason to doubt their authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, what we will do is perhaps that will take a little time because they are all in separate places.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We will simply, as I go through these documents, judge, if you could indicate if on any occasion when you look at them you either have doubts about the signature or the authenticity and that way it's probably the simplest way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words the procedure that we are going to follow, judge, is the following: Unless, when you're shown these documents, unless you tell us, "I don't -- I have doubts as to the authenticity of this document," we are going to take it that you consider those documents as authentic. In other words that you are recognising the signature and you're recognising the stamp, if there is a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Agenda, definition of the procedure regarding the order by the Banja Luka regional Secretariat for National Defence. Was that a reference to the order which had been issued on the 4th of May by Lieutenant Colonel Sajic in respect of mobilisation and curfew and the like? Perhaps you better look at this time 227, the very first decision. If you hang on a moment, it's going to be given to you or should be given to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you look at the very first decision, you turn over and you can see Lieutenant Colonel Sajic's name as the secretary, dated the 4th of May. It orders mobilisation and then four -- then 3, wartime schedules, 4, curfew, 5, "all paramilitary formations and individuals who illegally possess weapons and ammunition are to immediately, and by 1500 hours on the 11th of May, at the latest, surrender them to the municipal headquarters?"

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. Can I get an exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if you go on in that, the gazettes, you will see the deadline is extended, if you go, please, to number 7, the session of the 11th of May, the conclusions there, the deadline for the surrender of illegally acquired weapons has been extended to the 14th of May. Now, was that, to your recollection, judge, was that discussed in this meeting of the 15th of May, when it says definition of the procedure regarding the order?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember what was being discussed then?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: At this meeting, at which I was the note-taker, this discussion was about specific requests of the army command which was forwarded to us through the Secretariat for National Defence of the AR Krajina, because they are taken over the manner in which they worked from the former state and its army organisation. So that we were to send some men to the area of Kupres where the units of the Serb army were. Moreover, the mobilisation was already done and over in our case, at the time when this body is ordering the general and public mobilisation of the rest. So that what we are dealing with here and I believe I've told you about it, the veterinary medicine services, the medical service, had to be somehow reinforced. There were difficulties in clearing the grounds because there were many bodies, many people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: And there was livestock wandering about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we will come on to that a little later. We'll see the livestock problem in a moment. I agree you've already dealt with the fact that you'd already mobilised, but there was an order, was there not, that there should be a disarmament of persons who possessed weapons, paramilitaries, as it was described?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. It existed, and if you want me to, I'll explain what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all can we just -- deal with that, was that, do you remember, getting an order, originally from the national -- the Secretariat of National Defence of the autonomous region with deadlines subsequently being extended that what is described as paramilitary formations and individuals illegally possessing weapons being disarmed?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Yes. There were orders of that type, and also I heard it raised in discussions so there were deadlines for disarmament and I know that they were extended.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, the only question was: Was that something -- you've told us you discussed the orders that have come through about supplies to the army but do you remember that being discussed at this meeting of the 15th of May?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Why, yes. It was on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And we'll look at a document where you deal with how Petrovac dealt with that disarmament order in a moment but can you go, please, to item 2, the discussion of -- I'm sorry, it's actually quite complicated, it's decisions, they have conclusions and then decisions, and under decisions it's at page 4 of the document for us. "Shooting in public places and all other shooting are strictly prohibited because such a misuse of ammunition endangers security and jeopardises the defence capacity of the Serbian people." That's what was written here. You've already described how shooting was a problem. Was that the real reason, as given here, as to why shooting was to be prohibited? Because were you charged with carrying out this task.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I was made responsible together with other colleagues for misdemeanour, that is for the definition of misdemeanours and these petty offences fell under our -- under the municipal jurisdiction. That is specific to our system. And this here prescribes the penalties for the perpetrators of such petty offences. The real reason, well, here we see that it diminishes the combat preparedness and the waste of ammunition. But that was of lesser importance. The chief reason was that such behaviour of either individuals or groups who did that disturbed significantly the public peace and order and it also affected the feeling of security of citizens. People felt intimidated, especially the Muslims, but Serbs too, because any citizen who could not resist such behaviour had reason to be -- to feel intimidated, to feel afraid, and I think it was very distressful for Muslims, so they submitted written requests asking that this be put an end to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: And they voiced their fears.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. What I really want to know is why did you feel -- if that was the real reason, why was it necessary to give a reason that it was actually a misuse of ammunition, jeopardising the defence capacity, in other words that you were wasting ammunition? Why not put the real reason?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: The real reason is not indicated for political considerations. Had the real reason been indicated, that is that it was because of the fear that the Muslims felt, a vast majority of citizens would not have been happy with such a position of the municipal administration. Secondly, people who indulged in such activities were not really model citizens and they would have then said that the authorities were doing it to protect Muslims. And it was thought that if we did it in this way, we would leave them without that cause of discontent and that thereby we would manage to find or to establish grounds for their prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in the next decision, we can deal with that quite briefly, you and Mr. Sikman and Mr. Sepa were to form a commission to draw up proposal for insignia to display -- to be -- which will be displayed publicly and ways of displaying the Serbian flags blah, blah, sorry, not blah blah, and so on and so forth, ending up with change of town and street names. Did that happen? Was there a change of names and insignia? Just answer that fairly briefly, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Some of the changes were carried out, some were not. I know that the high street, which -- where the municipal hall was and so on and so forth, our institutions was renamed from Marsal Tito to St. Sava, perhaps there would have been more changes but in the assembly, councilmen disagreed regarding various proposals, and Mr. Sikman was there ex officio as the second of the assembly I was there as the legal expert and Sepa was the head of the general administrative affairs department and actually it was his department's job.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But -- that's all right. Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't answered about the insignia yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The insignia, was that changed?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I was about to answer that part. I was made responsible for thinking up the insignia for the vehicles used by the army. And I improvised it in a way. I saw a vehicle with a -- with some new markings and it was a triangle and in it were letters which said either the Serb army or the Army of Republika Srpska or something like that, and I just copied it and asked a clerk to make those markings, those symbols, those emblems and we then put them on our vehicles to indicate they had been requisitioned, both so that at the checkpoints somebody wouldn't seize that particular vehicle or requisition it, mobilise it once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That's all I want to ask you about that document. Can you look now, please, at P1842 which is a report to the assembly on the work of the Bosanski Petrovac SJB. Now, was one of the powers that the assembly had to call for a report from the SJB on its activities?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: One of the powers, yes. The assembly was to receive reports, also to comments on those reports, to make objections, and possibly request certain measures from higher police instances but yes, this was one of the original powers of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, it's an undated, unsigned report. You had a chance, I think, to read it or to look at it at the time of the interview. Was that a document that you had seen before? In other words, at the time that it was written? Whenever that may have been.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: I was not supposed to see this report in terms of the regular procedure. I was the secretary of the executive board. And this was intended for parliamentary debate. And I wasn't there unless I was asked to be there. What I can say is that I know from other sources that weapons of similar type were being seized.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Those were mostly hunting weapons, and some of the army weapons were also found.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But if we look at this report very briefly in the last five minutes, it's the police reporting on the disarmament operation ordered apparently because, it says, the CSB in Banja Luka, described as the most professionally conducted operation, completely broke up the SDA. In addition to the seizure of illegal and legal weapons, through its painstaking efforts, the public security station took a series of planned and organised operational measures and so on and so forth. Detaining persons who possessed illegal types of long-barrelled firearms, isolating persons who had demonstrated extremist views with respect to the policies of the Serbian people. And then it lists the various arms that were recovered, of which - and bullets as well - if we look at the list, it appears that most of the weaponry recovered was legally owned. In reality, was -- were the people being disarmed the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Well, I think judging by the circumstances, I do think that it was the non-Serbs who were disarmed by and large. Possibly that some of this weaponry, especially the army weaponry, were also seized from Serbs who were involved in excesses, but the hunting weapons, at least as far as I know about that time, they were mostly -- such weaponry was mostly seized from Muslims, and as a rule, their hunting weapons were licensed. They all had their licences for such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO
utterances.text: Another source that I know, and I mentioned it, at that time, and later, the police regularly, and I mean almost -- submitted almost daily reports regarding their operations relative to what went on on the ground. So that I learned about this in a different way. Why there is no signature on this text, well, probably this was merely an original document which was copied for the councilmen and they were about 50 of them. So to -- what they did was merely copy this document, I mean whoever on the assembly staff did it, they merely copied the document and deliver it to the councilmen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you have -- I take it that you have no reason to doubt the authenticity of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I haven't read this document either now or before but as for the seizure of weapons I have no reason to think it not being authentic so, yes, I think that this is authentic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's an appropriate moment. Your Honour, I'm sorry but I will take the whole of tomorrow. I understand that will still leave Mr. Cunningham sufficient time to cross-examine on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham, of course, you have time to think how much time you require for your cross-examination, and you will have all the time that you require.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will adjourn. Judge, we will meet again tomorrow morning at 9.00 and I suppose it has already been explained to you that in all probability you'll have to stay the weekend here and then you will finish on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.45 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 25th day of July, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
